title: Social media making it harder for UK parents to raise families, survey finds
summary:
Poll of parents of young children finds three-quarters think pressure from influencers has increased their anxiety

Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media…

blocks.text: Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media influencers to be “the perfect parent” is making it harder to raise a family, according to a survey.

Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”.

What information to trust also emerged as an issue, with almost half (49%) concerned about conflicting online advice. While one in five (21%) said they were using AI tools such as ChatGPT for parenting information, only 12% trusted it.

There was also a lack of trust in official advice. Almost half (48%) thought it was harder to trust professionals’ advice than it was for previous generations, with many relying on their own instincts and online research instead.

Many of those who participated took the view that parenting today was more difficult than in the past – 66% said children’s needs were more complex, yet 71% believed parents today had a better understanding of their children’s needs.

Families who had a child with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) faced greater challenges – 69% reported difficulty accessing professional support, compared with 31% of non-Send families and 64% had struggled to understand information about services compared with 28%.

The survey also reveals parents living in social isolation without a safety network. One in eight (12%) had nobody outside their immediate household they could call on at an hour’s notice in an emergency. The risk of isolation is higher for social housing tenants and parents whose first language is not English.

About 3,500 parents of children aged five and under took part in the 2026 National Early Childhood Parenting Survey by the early years charity Kindred Squared, which also includes a range of parents’ voices drawn from focus groups.

On lack of trust in professional advice, one parent in the south-east said: “I feel like nowadays, your GP doesn’t really know you as much any more. Everything feels rushed, basically. You kind of have to diagnose yourself before you go to them.”

On social media pressures, a London parent said: “I was feeling this pressure to be perfect. You have to be perfect in everything. I think social media influencers really get into your head and make you think it’s possible to be that way, but in reality, it’s not.”

A parent in the south-west disagreed: “For me personally, social media did not increase my anxiety around parenting. They make it easier … It takes the pressure away from me and just lets me enjoy the moment.”

The survey, published on Thursday, suggests parenting has changed significantly in the space of a generation. “I love my parents,” said a West Midlands parent, “but they have no idea what it is like bringing up a child in 2026 … they don’t quite understand that it’s not as simple.”

“For me, I would say it’s different in the sense that we’re more emotionally aware of what’s happening with our children, with ourselves,” a parent in the south-west said. “Whereas I feel like the older generation … you just get on with it basically.”

Felicity Gillespie, Kindred’s chief executive, said the survey showed that most parents felt capable of looking after young children but the “levels of isolation, the feeling of being under pressure and the lack of trust in official advice are all striking”.

She went on: “I think this report clearly sets out that, for many parents, they feel that the task of raising children is tougher today than in previous generations.

“I hope these findings will inform policymakers at all levels who have a role in supporting parents and families because it’s quite clear that families with the youngest children need trustworthy, easy-to-access advice, the space to be the parents they want to be and, above all, we need to remove that overriding fear of being judged or being all alone.”

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We want every child to have the best start in life, and that means supporting parents too with practical advice alongside measures to give families breathing space with the cost of living. That’s why we are giving working parents 30 hours of childcare, saving some families up to £8,000 a year.
“We’re also investing £900m for Best Start Family Hubs across England, giving parents a trusted place in their community for parenting support and help with their child’s health and development.
“Building on the proud legacy of Sure Start, we’re bringing early education, advice and support closer to families and giving children stronger foundations to thrive.”
